summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for 10/20/30 rule (Kawasaki); source-anchored research pack.

facts.text: 14. **The rule's subject narrowed from "a PowerPoint presentation" (2005) to "a pitch" (2015).** The post "The Only 10 Slides You Need in Your Pitch" (published 5 March 2015, last modified 12 October 2021) opens: "I am evangelizing the 10/20/30 Rule of PowerPoint. It's quite simple: a pitch should have ten slides, last no more than twenty minutes, and contain no font smaller than thirty points." Source: https://guykawasaki.com/the-only-10-slides-you-need-in-your-pitch/

15. **In its current form the ten-topic list has been removed from Kawasaki's post body and replaced by a downloadable Canva template.** The 2021-modified version of "The Only 10 Slides You Need in Your Pitch" contains only the three bullets (ten slides, twenty minutes, thirty-point font) plus an embedded Canva design and a "Download This Template" button pointing at https://www.canva.com/design/DAEhUeYe_fo/view — so the canonical ten-slide list now lives in a design asset, not in prose. Source: https://guykawasaki.com/the-only-10-slides-you-need-in-your-pitch/

**Claim 8 — The "roughly ten topics" element is independently corroborated by primary VC guidance.** Sequoia Capital's own writing-a-business-plan guide enumerates exactly ten elements — company purpose, problem, solution, why now, market potential, competition, business model, team, financials, vision (https://www.sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/). Sequoia arrived at ten topics independently of Kawasaki and gives no slide-count or brevity instruction at all, which suggests the durable part of "10" is *ten subjects to cover*, not *ten physical slides*.

**A5.** The same original post contains a second, incompatible font rule: "find out the age of the oldest person in your audience and divide it by two. That's your optimal font size." For any audience whose oldest member is under 60, this algorithm prescribes a font *below* thirty points, contradicting the rule's own floor. Kawasaki does not reconcile the two.

This report covers only the 10/20/30 rule as formulated by Guy Kawasaki: ten slides, twenty minutes, thirty-point minimum font. It traces where the rule was first published, how its wording and stated rationale changed across Kawasaki's own publications, and what independent evidence supports or contradicts it. Sibling pitch-deck concepts (Sequoia's template, DocSend's deck structure, the parent Pitch Deck Writing domain) appear only where they directly confirm or disconfirm a 10/20/30 claim; they are not researched here.

3. **The rule's exact original wording is: "a PowerPoint presentation should have ten slides, last no more than twenty minutes, and contain no font smaller than thirty points."** Kawasaki explicitly generalises it beyond fundraising in the same paragraph: "While I'm in the venture capital business, this rule is applicable for any presentation to reach agreement: for example, raising capital, making a sale, forming a partnership, etc." Source: https://guykawasaki.com/the_102030_rule/

12. **By *The Art of the Start 2.0* (2015) the rule is called "The 10/20/30 Rule of Presentations".** Open Library's scan of *The Art of the Start 2.0* contains "The 10/20/30 Rule of Presentations is that you should use ten…"; Kawasaki's 9 March 2015 post "The Art of the Pitch" carries the same phrasing and states "This post is a tiny part of Guy Kawasaki's latest book, The Art of the Start 2.0." Sources: https://openlibrary.org/search/inside?q=%2210%2F20%2F30+Rule%22 and https://guykawasaki.com/the-art-of-the-pitch/

This report covers only the 10/20/30 rule as formulated by Guy Kawasaki: what its three parts are, what mechanism each part is claimed to operate by, what conditions the rule assumes, and where it breaks. It does not cover sibling pitch-deck heuristics, general presentation design, or the wider Pitch Deck Writing domain. Kawasaki's ten-slide content list is treated here only as a component of the rule, not as a topic in its own right.

Two evidentiary limits apply throughout. First, `guykawasaki.com` and `docsend.com` both return HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so claims sourced to those hosts are taken from search-engine extracts or from third-party hosts that reproduce the text; they are marked `[indirect]`. Second, there is no peer-reviewed study that tests the 10/20/30 rule as a unit. Every empirical claim below tests one of its three components, or a premise it rests on, not the rule as a package. That absence is itself the central finding.

**C3.** Ten slides and ten concepts are not the same quantity, and the rule conflates them. Cognitive-load research on slide design finds that splitting content across more, simpler slides lowers perceived cognitive workload; the assertion-evidence structure (one sentence assertion plus visual evidence per slide) produced significantly better comprehension and recall than topic-headline-plus-bullets slides (p < .01). Under that structure, holding to ten slides *increases* per-slide density and works against comprehension. Sources: http://writing.engr.psu.edu/2005_alley_neeley.pdf · https://pee

**G3.** The "obvious at a glance" goal that the thirty-point floor serves is endorsed by YC on independent grounds: a slide should be understandable at a glance, because investors who do not get the point immediately disengage. The mechanism is confirmed even though the specific point size is not (E1–E3).

7. **Thirty points is justified by the read-ahead desync problem and by forcing preparation.** "as soon as the audience figures out that you're reading the text, it reads ahead of you because it can read faster than you can speak. The result is that you and the audience are out of synch." Kawasaki adds that small fonts signal "they don't know their material well enough" and that "more text is more convincing. Total bozosity." Source: https://guykawasaki.com/the_102030_rule/

14. Practitioners who keep the rule handle this by treating twenty minutes as the longest of several rehearsed lengths — being able to deliver the same deck in 5, 10 and 20 minutes, because meeting times are unpredictable. (https://kruzeconsulting.com/blog/guy-kawasaki-pitch-deck-the-ultimate-guide/)

16. The second mechanism is the load-bearing one: a large font physically caps how much text fits on a slide, which forces the presenter to find the salient points and stops the audience reading ahead of the speaker. Kawasaki calls the belief that "more text is more convincing" "total bozosity." (https://www.presentationmagazine.com/the-10-20-30-rule-of-powerpoint-11710.htm)

30. The rule survives its own falsified premises because its value is behavioural, not predictive. Each number makes a specific bad habit mechanically harder: sixty-slide decks, monologues that eat the whole slot, and paragraph-dense slides. That is why sources that dispute all three numbers still recommend the rule as a heuristic. (https://sixminutes.dlugan.com/10-20-30-rule-guy-kawasaki-powerpoint/, https://www.pitchdeckstudios.com/blog/the-10-20-30-rule-does-it-still-apply-to-modern-pitch-decks)

4. **Brevity predicts engagement, not funding.** `edge-cases.md` carries both findings without reconciling them. Completion drops ~20 points from 8→16 pages, but successful pre-seed decks were viewed 3m21s and unsuccessful ones 3m30s, and 60% of successful teams had *longer*-than-average decks. Any recommendation built on the rule should claim the first and not the second.

**E1.** Point size alone cannot specify legibility; only angular size can. Legge and Bigelow's review in *Journal of Vision* (2011, 11(5):8) specifies print size in angular units and puts the fluent reading range at roughly 0.2°–2° of x-height, which at a 40 cm reading distance corresponds to physical x-heights of about 4 to 40 points. A "30 point" slide subtends a different visual angle depending on projection size and viewing distance, so the rule is under-specified as stated.

**G2.** The rule's target for what the audience should retain is close to correct, and arguably still too generous. YC independently converges on 5–7 memorable ideas (C2), and Cowan's 3–5 chunk limit (C1) sits just below that. 2. **"Kawasaki scoped it to VC pitches" is wrong, and three of four reports assert it.** The primary text generalises in the same paragraph: *"this rule is applicable for any presentation to reach agreement: for example, raising capital, making a sale, forming a partnership."* But that's a persuasion boundary, not a blanket one — it still excludes the lectures and workshops `edge-cases.md` catalogues as out-of-domain transfer. Defensible scope: persuasive presentations seeking a decision.

This report covers only Guy Kawasaki's 10/20/30 rule: the prescription that a pitch presentation use no more than ten slides, run no longer than twenty minutes, and set no font smaller than thirty points. It examines where each of the three numbers holds, where it breaks, what its stated rationale rests on, and what evidence contradicts it.

**A1.** The rule is three simultaneous constraints: ten slides, twenty minutes, no font below thirty points. Kawasaki published it on 2005-12-30 and has promoted it continuously since. Source: https://guykawasaki.com/the_102030_rule/ `[indirect]`

**A6.** Kawasaki has not revised the rule. He restated it verbatim on 2025-09-03: "Let's not forget the 10/20/30 rule: 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point font. It's not just a guideline—it's a survival strategy."

5. **Whether the rule should be scoped out of non-VC use.** A2 scopes it to VC pitches; F4 documents it being applied to lectures and training. No source found states an authoritative boundary, and Kawasaki's own site and Substack present it as applying to "a PowerPoint presentation" generally.

**A4.** The thirty-point number is a forcing function, not a legibility threshold. Kawasaki's argument is that a large font makes dense text impossible: "Force yourself to use no font smaller than thirty points... The reason people use a small font is twofold: first, they don't know their material well enough; second, they think that more text is more convincing."

**B1.** Observed successful decks are roughly twice as long as the rule allows. The DocSend / Tom Eisenmann (Harvard Business School) study of 200+ startups that together raised more than $360M found the average successful seed and Series A deck ran about 19 pages.

**B4.** The same dataset shows a real brevity effect, but located at a different boundary than ten: completion rate falls about 20 points between 8-page and 16-page decks. This supports "short," and simultaneously places the optimum above the rule's cap.

**E5.** That disfluency finding does not survive cleanly, so E4 should not be read as positive evidence against large fonts — only as evidence that the legibility-to-retention link the rule assumes is not established. A dedicated special issue of *Metacognition and Learning* (2016) reporting direct and conceptual replications found null effects of disfluency on learning outcomes. Sources: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11409-015-9151-5 · https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x

**F1.** Density displacement. Capping slide count without capping content pushes content onto fewer slides, which the thirty-point floor then forbids — so founders either break the font rule or delete substance. The rule provides no resolution for this collision, and C3 indicates the resolution it implicitly picks (fewer, denser slides) is the worse one for comprehension. Sources: http://writing.engr.psu.edu/2005_alley_neeley.pdf · https://www.koad.com/post/why-you-shouldnt-bother-with-the-10-20-30-rule

**F4.** Out-of-domain transfer. The rule is widely quoted for academic lectures, technical deep-dives, and instructional workshops, which is outside the VC-pitch context of A2 and where typical slide counts run 20–30.

**G1.** The rule's directional claim — shorter is better — is supported. Both large deck-analytics datasets find brevity pays: completion falls sharply with added pages (B4), and short decks are over-represented among successful teams (B5).
